label: Yesha'yahu (Isaiah) — 1QIsa-a — Part 3 — Chapters 28–41
summary_plain: Yesha'yahu pronounces woe upon Ephrayim and the drunkards of Shomron. YHWH lays in Tsiyon a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation — whoever believes will not be in haste. Woe to those who go down to Mitsrayim for help and rely on horses. A king will reign in righteousness. The wilderness will become a fruitful field. Comfort, comfort my people, says your Creator. Every valley shall be lifted up and every mountain brought low. The nations are like a drop from a bucket. YHWH gives power to the faint and strengthens the powerless. Those who wait upon YHWH shall renew their strength — they shall mount up with wings as eagles.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and the Orit Ge'ez. The cornerstone passage (28:16) is read by the Qumran community in the Community Rule (1QS 8:7) as referring to the community itself — the tested foundation laid by YHWH. The comfort oracle beginning in chapter 40 marks the transition in tone from judgment to restoration. 1QIsa-a preserves this transition as a continuous scroll — the same scribe, the same manuscript. The artificial division of 'First Isaiah' and 'Second Isaiah' by Western scholarship has no basis in the Qumran manuscript evidence. The scroll is one document.

key_terms.definition: Yesha'yahu 40 opens the section known as Deutero-Yesha'yahu with the double call 'Comfort, comfort my people'; it marks a shift from judgment to consolation, addressing those in Babylonian exile.
The opening cry of Yesha'yahu 40: YHWH commands double comfort for his people; their warfare is ended and their iniquity is pardoned.
Yesha'yahu 40:3 — 'A voice cries: In the wilderness prepare the way of YHWH; make straight in the desert a highway for our Creator.' This ancient Hebrew text is the source; the NT borrowed from it.

Sennakherib's siege of Yerushalayim and Khizkiyahu's illness and recovery dominate Yesha'yahu 36-39; YHWH delivers the city but Khizkiyahu's foolish display to Babylonian envoys seals Yehudah's future exile.
Yesha'yahu 40:31 — 'Those who wait for YHWH shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.'
Yesha'yahu 40 describes YHWH as one whose arm rules for him — feeding the flock like a shepherd and gathering the lambs; his arm carries the creation.
Yesha'yahu 28 opens with 'Woe to the proud crown of the drunkards of Efrayim'; six woes follow in chapters 28-33 addressing faithless leaders, false alliances, and trust in Mitzrayim instead of YHWH.

key_terms.term: He Who Created You O Ya'akov
key_terms.definition: Yesha'yahu 43:1 — 'Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.' YHWH addresses Yisra'el as the one who formed and redeemed them.
Yesha'yahu 40-41 mocks idol-making: a craftsman cuts down a tree, uses half for fire and half to make an idol, then bows to it. The polemic exposes the emptiness of manufactured deities.
Yesha'yahu 21 depicts a sentinel posted to watch for Babylon's fall; when the news comes — 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon' — the sentinel reports it to Yehudah.

faq.question: What is the 'Comfort Prologue' and why does it mark a shift in Yesha'yahu?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 40 opens with 'Comfort, comfort my people' — a double call that signals a shift from judgment (chapters 1-39) to consolation. Scholars call chapters 40-55 Deutero-Yesha'yahu because the audience is no longer Ahaz or Khizkiyahu's era but exiles in Babylon. YHWH's comfort is based on his identity as Creator and Redeemer.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yesha'yahu 40:3 as an ancient source text?
faq.answer: The cry 'A voice in the wilderness: prepare the way of YHWH' in Yesha'yahu 40:3 is an ancient Hebrew prophetic text. The NT borrowed its language. The ancient text is the source; it does not derive from the NT. Its context in Yesha'yahu is specifically the return of exiles from Babylon, not a distant messianic figure.

faq.question: Why is Khizkiyahu's show to the Babylonian envoys significant?
faq.answer: In Yesha'yahu 39, Khizkiyahu shows all his treasury, armory, and storehouses to Babylonian envoys who come to congratulate him after his recovery. Yesha'yahu immediately pronounces that everything Khizkiyahu showed will be carried to Babylon. This is the pivot point linking Khizkiyahu's era to the coming exile.

faq.question: What is the Molten Image Polemic in Yesha'yahu 40-44?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 40-44 contains a sustained polemic against idol-making. The craftsman plants a tree; rain nourishes it; he cuts it down, uses half for fire and warmth, and from the other half carves a god to bow down to. The polemic's point: the idol is wood; YHWH created the earth with his outstretched hand and weighs the mountains in a balance.

faq.question: What does the eagle-wings imagery in Yesha'yahu 40:31 convey?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 40:31 promises that those who wait (or hope) for YHWH will have their strength renewed; they will rise up on wings like eagles, run without exhaustion, and walk without fainting. The eagle's ability to soar effortlessly on thermals captures the contrast between human exhaustion and the energy YHWH gives to those who trust him.

faq.question: What are the six woes of Yesha'yahu 28-33?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 28-33 contains six woe-oracles: (1) Woe to Efrayim's proud drunkards (28); (2) Woe to Ariel/Yerushalayim (29); (3) Woe to those who hide plans from YHWH (29:15); (4) Woe to those who go down to Mitzrayim for help (31); (5) Woe to the destroyer who has not been destroyed (33); and (6) Woe to those who make a covenant with Mitzrayim but not with YHWH's spirit (30).

faq.question: How did YHWH deliver Yerushalayim from Sennakherib in Yesha'yahu 37?
faq.answer: After Khizkiyahu spread Sennakherib's letter before YHWH in the Temple and prayed, YHWH answered through Yesha'yahu: Sennakherib will not enter the city or shoot an arrow there. That night, the messenger of YHWH struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. Sennakherib departed and was later killed by his own sons in Nineveh.

faq.question: What argument does Yesha'yahu 40 make for YHWH's incomparability?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 40:12-26 stacks rhetorical questions: Who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand? Who weighed the mountains? Who counseled YHWH? Who taught him? Then: Who stretches the heavens like a curtain? Who brings out the starry host by number? The answer is always YHWH alone — no nation, no idol, no heavenly advisor is his equal.

faq.question: What is the foundation stone laid in Tziyon in Yesha'yahu 28:16?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 28:16 — contrasting the false 'covenant with death' the leaders made — says YHWH is laying in Tziyon a tested cornerstone, a sure foundation. 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.' This stone is the covenant community's true security, opposed to the false security of an alliance with Mitzrayim.

faq.question: Why does Yesha'yahu 40 emphasize YHWH as Creator?
faq.answer: The exiles in Babylon saw the great temples of Marduk and Babylon's military power. Yesha'yahu 40 counters this: YHWH alone created the heavens by stretching them out, sustains the stars by name, and weighs the nations as dust on a scale. The Creator argument grounds YHWH's ability to redeem the exiles — if he made everything, Babylon's power is nothing before him.
